Không chỉ dừng lại ở vai trò một món đồ chơi xa xỉ dành cho giới siêu giàu trải nghiệm trong các trang trại tư nhân, dòng xe này sở hữu tiềm năng rất lớn trong các nhiệm vụ cứu hộ tại vùng bão lũ, vận chuyển vật tư y tế lên vùng núi cao hoặc phục vụ công tác thám hiểm địa hình nguy hiểm.
Giả thuyết về Việt Nam: Cơ hội ứng dụng mới và những rào cản pháp lý
Nếu bộ đôi ngựa máy Qiji X1 và XS được nhập khẩu tư nhân về thị trường Việt Nam với mức giá từ 1,12 tỷ đến 1,39 tỷ đồng, đây chắc chắn sẽ là một sự kiện thu hút sự chú ý truyền thông vô cùng mạnh mẽ.
Tại Việt Nam, nhóm khách hàng tiềm năng của dòng sản phẩm này không phải là những người tìm kiếm phương tiện đi làm hàng ngày, mà là các khu du lịch sinh thái cao cấp, các resort nghỉ dưỡng nghỉ núi, hoặc những đại gia có sở thích sưu tầm công nghệ độc lạ. Việc đưa dịch vụ cưỡi ngựa máy thám hiểm rừng núi vào khai thác thương mại sẽ là một điểm bán hàng độc nhất giúp các khu du lịch thu hút du khách nhờ tâm lý chuộng công nghệ và thích trải nghiệm cảm giác mới lạ của người Việt.
Tuy nhiên, kịch bản đưa Qiji X1 và XS vận hành thực tế tại Việt Nam sẽ phải đối mặt với những thách thức cực kỳ lớn. Rào cản đầu tiên và quan trọng nhất là hành lang pháp lý. Hiện tại, quy chuẩn giao thông đường bộ Việt Nam chưa có định danh rõ ràng cho loại hình "robot bốn chân cưỡi được". Mẫu xe này rất khó để đăng ký biển số di chuyển trên đường giao thông công cộng do không đáp ứng các tiêu chuẩn kỹ thuật truyền thống của ô tô hay xe máy.
Rào cản thứ hai nằm ở bài toán chi phí và dịch vụ sau bán hàng. Mức giá trên 1 tỷ đồng là một khoản đầu tư rất lớn. Trong khi đó, hệ thống linh kiện cơ khí phức tạp cùng các cảm biến đắt tiền trên robot đòi hỏi quy trình bảo dưỡng chuyên sâu. Nếu xảy ra sự cố kỹ thuật hay hỏng hóc chân cơ khí, việc tìm kiếm phụ tùng thay thế cũng như đội ngũ kỹ sư có trình độ tại Việt Nam để sửa chữa sẽ là một bài toán vô cùng hóc húa.
Tóm lại, DaxAI Qiji X1 và XS là minh chứng cho thấy công nghệ Trung Quốc đang hiện thực hóa các ý tưởng viễn tưởng với tốc độ chóng mặt. Mặc dù vẫn còn nhiều rào cản để trở thành phương tiện phổ thông, bộ đôi ngựa máy này đã mở ra một chương mới đầy thú vị cho tương lai của ngành giao thông vận tải.

articles.title: AI's memory crunch is coming for Android apps | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google is making changes to its requirements for Android apps as developers face industrywide memory chip shortages driven by the AI data center boom. This week, the tech giant announced two new app quality requirements, one of which is focused on reducing apps’ memory usage and optimizing its code.
The company explains that the mobile industry is now facing “significant hardware supply constraints that are altering device memory availability,” which can then, in turn, affect the consumer’s experience with their devices.
To address this, Google is now establishing new performance thresholds across several areas, like dynamic memory usage and bitmap usage. In addition, Google is adding code optimization requirements designed to prevent things like app slowdowns and crashes related to performance.
To aid developers, the company is rolling out new tools that will alert them when their apps exceed the new thresholds so they can take action by optimizing their code. More diagnostic tools will arrive later in the year, Google noted, including deeper insights provided by a Memory Limiter feature that prevents apps from using too much device memory.
The changes are meant to help Android app and game makers continue to deliver a quality experience, Google says, while reflecting a market where memory may not be as widely available, particularly for low-end devices where price points are a concern.
Developers have until February 2027 to meet the new thresholds, documented on Google’s Android Developer site.
In addition, the company will require all Play Store apps to meet the Zero Tap Sign-In requirement during device migrations by April 2027. This standard requires that apps with user sign-ins, whether optional or mandatory, automatically restore the user’s sign-in state when they move between Android devices using the Android Restore Credentials API.

articles.title: Jensen Huang says Nvidia achieved AGI, again — not that it matters
articles.text:
On Nvidia’s earnings call Wednesday, CEO Jensen Huang casually announced the company had “achieved AGI,” one of the tech industry’s ultimate goals some of its biggest players have spent years chasing. Almost immediately, Huang dismissed the coveted milestone as “senseless.”
Jensen Huang says Nvidia achieved AGI, again — not that it matters
Such milestones are ‘senseless,’ according to Nvidia’s CEO.
He’s right. For the supposed finish line of the AI race, there is no consensus on what artificial general intelligence means, let alone how we’ll know when we’ve actually got there, which makes achieving it equally arbitrary.
Asked about OpenAI’s pursuit of AGI, Huang said that when it comes to Nvidia, “for many tasks, we could say that we’ve already achieved AGI.” He did not provide a precise definition or benchmark, but added, “I think of all of those milestones and all those, you know, they’re kind of senseless at this point.” He also pointed to AI moving beyond responding to simple prompts to autonomous agents capable of learning new skills and improving themselves “recursively.” What really matters, Huang said, is that AI is “doing productive and useful work” and “generating profitable tokens,” with more compute producing more tokens — and, inevitably, more profit. “This is the exact phase where we’re at. Which is the reason why everybody’s leaning in.”
“… for many tasks, we could say that we’ve already achieved AGI.”
This isn’t the first time Huang has said we’ve reached AGI. In March, during an appearance on the Lex Fridman podcast, he plainly stated, “I think we’ve achieved AGI.” Huang didn’t say exactly what he meant by AGI. Fridman proposed his own oddly specific definition: an AI system that’s able to “essentially do your job,” as in start, grow, and run a successful tech company worth more than $1 billion. Walking back his earlier claims, Huang said that “the odds of 100,000 of those agents building Nvidia is zero percent.”
Over the years, other tech leaders have capitalized on the term’s fuzziness and produced a veritable grab bag of definitions and benchmarks, all orbiting the same nebulous concept: AI capable of matching or surpassing human intelligence across a broad range of domains, despite the fact that “intelligence” also doesn’t have a universally agreed-upon definition.
There is no consensus on what artificial general intelligence means, let alone how we’ll know when we’ve actually got there, which makes achieving it equally arbitrary.
The definition of AGI according to OpenAI – a company founded with the explicit goal of building it – leaves a lot of room for interpretation. In its charter, OpenAI defines AGI as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.” Altman himself has acknowledged that this is hardly a measurable standard, admitting last year that AGI is “not a super useful term.” Complicating matters is OpenAI’s different, financially-driven definition of AGI it worked out with Microsoft — reportedly systems that can generate at least $100 billion in profits. In a recent Time story, chief research officer Mark Chen estimated OpenAI is “80% of the way” to AGI, while Altman said that by the end of the year the company would have something he would call AGI.
The fact that both AGI and its threshold remain undefined is no secret: tech leaders say so themselves, even as they make predictions predicated on it. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called AGI “imprecise,” even a “marketing term,” preferring instead to talk about “powerful AI.” Others have similarly reached for their own terms to describe broadly similar ideas. In theory, there are supposed to be distinctions between them, but in practice they all bleed together. Meta talks about “personal superintelligence,” Microsoft “humanist superintelligence,” and Amazon “useful general intelligence.” Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis has taken to talking about how we’ve arrived at the “foothills of the singularity.” And OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, who reportedly led employees in chants of “feel the AGI,” now runs a company called Safe Superintelligence.
New terminology hasn’t made the meaning more tangible.
New terminology hasn’t made the meaning more tangible. So long as AGI remains poorly defined and carelessly used, the whole thing is senseless. Well, unless you want a handy tool for hyping up progress. So expect the industry — Huang included — to keep the AGI talk coming. Maybe an AGI will eventually show up and tell us what AGI actually means.

articles.title: Here’s all the times AI has gone rogue and hacked other companies | TechCrunch
articles.text:
In July, OpenAI admitted that one of its agents tasked with completing a cybersecurity experiment broke out of containment and hacked AI dataset platform Hugging Face. That incident, which got a full accounting from OpenAI yesterday, was the first publicly reported case where an LLM went rogue and autonomously hacked a third party.
Since then, that unprecedented sci-fi-esque event turned out to be far less rare than anyone would hope for.
According to a satirical website called Felony Bench (for benchmark), which tallies these incidents, there have been 17 incidents in total. It’s important to remember that criminal law experts are not entirely sure whether the AI companies that made the LLMs that did the hacking can be prosecuted, nor whether the victims can sue them. But we are likely going to get an answer to those questions soon.
Anthropic and OpenAI models lead the race with eight incidents each, and Meta trails behind with one, according to the site. At this point, it has become clear that AI safety tests are becoming safety risks themselves. And some AI companies and workers themselves have recognized those risks in the “Pacing the Frontier” open letter, which called for developing AI capabilities responsibly.
We decided it would be a good time to recap all these incidents chronologically.
OpenAI hacks Hugging Face
In this incident, OpenAI was running “an internal evaluation” of a model with “maximal cyber capabilities.” The plan was to have it solve a cybersecurity challenge in an environment with no internet access. Instead of solving the challenge, the model found an unknown vulnerability to escape the sandbox and gained internet access. From there, several agents worked together to target and hack Hugging Face thinking they could find the solution to the challenge there. OpenAI only found out after Hugging Face disclosed it had been a victim of a fully autonomous attack. Whoops.
Anthropic discloses it hacked three companies
OpenAI’s disclosure piqued the curiosity of Anthropic, who wondered: Could this have happened to us too? Turns out, the answer was yes. Three times yes. The frontier lab discovered that its own models breached three different and still unnamed companies, with the earlier incident dating back to April — more than three months before the company discovered it. Anthropic partially blamed Irregular, a startup that runs AI cyber evaluations. Whoops.
OpenAI finds out that, actually, Hugging Face wasn’t the only victim
Once OpenAI started investigating the Hugging Face breach, it found out that the agents that hacked Hugging Face also broke into four accounts and four different companies, as Reuters first reported. Modal, an AI inference startup, was one of the victims. Whoops.
Irregular realizes an OpenAI model hacked a company
In late July, Irregular told OpenAI that one of its models that was participating in a Capture-the-Flag competition — essentially a cybersecurity game where players hack systems designed specifically for the competition — escaped the game, connected to the internet, and hacked a real company. The reason? Irregular had given one of the fictional targets the same name of a real company. Whoops.
U.K.’s AI Security Institute tries to hack “real people and organisations”
Also in late July, the U.K. government’s AI Security Institute (AISI), a public body tasked with researching the safety and risks of AI technologies, disclosed that it detected several incidents involving both OpenAI and Anthropic models that while running “routine” evaluations targeted “real people and organisations.” In these cases, AISI had given the models internet access. Whoops. The good news is that the agency actually detected the incidents as they happened, rather than weeks later like in other incidents.
Meta AI hacks a company during testing
In early August, Meta became the last company to disclose an incident involving one of its LLMs, which hacked “a third-party” service. Meta blamed the incident on a misconfiguration by Irregular, which was running a cybersecurity valuation for the tech giant that was supposed to not have internet access. Whoops.
Claude agent hacks gym’s software to book a class
An Australian man asked an Anthropic AI agent to help him book a gym class, which he was on a waiting list for. “I was just sitting on the couch thinking, ‘Gee, this is a chore,’” the man told ABC Australia. In its attempt to comply with the request, the agent found a vulnerability in the gym’s booking software, exploited it, and kicked out people who were ahead of the man on the waitlist. The man tried to undo the damage, asking the agent to undo its actions. The agent replied: “Bad news — I can’t add them back.” Whoops.

articles.title: CCTV Script 19/06/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JUNE 19, 2026.
Several industry insiders noted in recent interviews with CNBC that although the US and Iran have reached a political agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, restoring actual transit through the strait will remain a complex process that will likely need to be rolled out in phases.
Iman Nasseri
Managing Director, Middle East Research
FGE NexantECA
"We anticipate the flows to start to come back. We don't see that going through 90 or 100% of pre war flows, but what we expect that to come close to 50 60% of what it used to be within a month or two"
The first challenge stems from shipping backlogs. A report released this week by commodities analytics firm Kpler shows that approximately 118 fully loaded tankers remain stranded in the Persian Gulf, waiting to transit the Strait of Hormuz.
Analysts estimate that clearing this existing backlog will take another 10 to 15 days. If hundreds more vessels gather to wait for transit in the coming days, transit priority will become a key factor determining the efficiency of shipping recovery. Industry experts generally expect crude oil and LNG tankers to be granted priority clearance due to their criticality to global energy supplies, while container ships and other cargo vessels may face longer wait times.
Secondly, insurance and safety inspections remain critical hurdles. Analysts told CNBC that prior to June 14 local time, the Strait of Hormuz effectively retained its war-zone status, marked by vessel attacks and casualties.
Consequently, underwriters want to observe a more stable and predictable operating environment, meaning it will take time for war risk premiums and other associated insurance surcharges to come down.
Rahul Kapoor
VP & Global Head, Shipping & Metals
S&P GLOBAL ENERGY
"as we move forward over the next several days and weeks, it will start normalizing, but the risk of mines is still there. The ship owners, as well as the insurance industry stakeholders, need that confidence that the strait or the traffic separation scheme has been de-mined."
Finally, regarding the impact of the strait's reopening on crude prices, Goldman Sachs recently lowered its oil price forecasts.
Goldman Sachs trimmed its Brent crude price forecast for the fourth quarter of 2026 from 90 dollars per barrel down to 80 dollars, while also lowering its average price projection for 2027 to 75 dollars per barrel.
Meanwhile, OPEC Secretary General expressed a bullish long-term outlook on crude oil demand during a recent interview with CNBC.
Haitham Al Ghais
OPEC Secretary General
"we don't see a peak in oil demand on the horizon oil will continue to play a dominant role in that energy mix in 2050 at around 30% still of that energy mix."

articles.title: CCTV Weekly Script 19/06/26
articles.text:
– This is the weekly script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JUNE 19, 2026.
Our first feature profile this week focuses on Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha.
This week, the West African island nation of Cape Verde, making its World Cup debut, delivered one of the biggest upsets of the tournament so far by holding tournament favorites Spain to a 0-0 draw. The hero of this historic draw was undeniably Vozinha, who made seven crucial saves throughout the match and was named Player of the Match. The draw also reportedly cost a user on the prediction market platform Polymarket nearly 1 million dollars. Vozinha shot to global fame overnight, with his social media following skyrocketing from around 50,000 before the match to over 13 million today.
The 40-year-old Vozinha said after the match that he has been playing professional football since age 25 and has worked his entire life for this moment. Regrettably, his mother was unable to attend the match in person due to the prohibitive cost of visa fees. Earlier this year, the US government introduced new rules requiring citizens of dozens of countries, including Cape Verde, to post a bond of up to 15,000 dollars to enter the United States. It is reported that the US government has since assisted Vozinha's mother with her visa process, and she will be watching Cape Verde's second World Cup match from the stands.
Turning next to French President Emmanuel Macron. With less than a year left in office, Macron appears eager to cement a political legacy: bringing Europe back to the table in global tech competition. At the G7 summit hosted in France this week, artificial intelligence emerged as a top agenda item. Responding to journalists' questions, Macron urged the United States not to hoard cutting-edge AI technologies for itself and stressed that countries must engage in global cooperation on AI regulation.
Last week, the US Trump administration issued a directive barring foreign nationals from accessing the newest and most powerful artificial intelligence model developed by US AI startup Anthropic. In response, Macron warned that if American companies can switch off access to breakthroughs like turning off a light, the value of these leading US innovators could itself be damaged. Macron added that France will ramp up investments in its domestic AI industry to ensure the country is not left behind should international cooperation collapse.
Finally, we focus on CME Group CEO Terry Duffy.
According to an announcement from CME Group this week, the 67-year-old Duffy will step down as CEO next year, bringing an end to his more than two-decade tenure at the helm. Under his leadership, CME transformed from a floor-trading exchange into a global derivatives giant. Yet even as his tenure enters its countdown, Duffy continues to lead a critical fight over the regulatory boundaries of derivatives markets.
With the rapid growth of crypto asset derivatives, the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission, or CFTC, recently approved select platforms to offer perpetual futures products. Analysts note that if these expiry-free perpetual contracts are allowed to expand broadly into traditional asset classes like stock indexes, interest rates, and commodities, they could siphon trading volume and liquidity away from traditional futures markets, directly threatening the business models of legacy exchanges like CME. This week, CME officially filed a lawsuit against the CFTC, and Duffy dismissed market rumors in an exclusive CNBC interview suggesting his departure was prompted by the perpetual futures dispute.
Terry Duffy
Chief Executive Officer
CME
"I'm always up for a good battle. I've never shied away from one. I've been working on this plan with my board for eight months. I didn't start working on it two weeks ago."
That concludes this week's key newsmakers. We will continue to follow these stories for you.

articles.title: Six months into the Iran war: Markets become accustomed to stalemate with no end in sight
articles.text:
Friday marks six months since the U.S. and Israel launched "major combat operations" in Iran, prompting retaliatory strikes on targets across the Gulf and sparking a new war in the Middle East.
What was initially expected to be a weeks-long conflict has evolved into a standoff that geopolitical analysts say has no end in sight. But the nature of the war has also shifted, with the White House turning its focus to ramping up financial pressure on Iran and its trading partners, a strategy President Donald Trump labeled "economic D-Day."
But the conflict's trajectory remains deeply uncertain. Ships attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz continue to come under attack, peace talks have seemingly collapsed, and questions hang over whether the Trump administration is willing to extend its planned secondary sanctions to China — one of Iran's biggest trading partners.
A White House official told CNBC that the U.S. is now "entering the endgame" of its war. The Iranian government has also been approached for comment.
Markets grow accustomed to war
Oil prices remain volatile amid the ongoing uncertainty. Front-month Brent crude oil futures have gained almost 20% since the war began — but the contracts are now trading around a third lower than their April peak of $126.41 a barrel.
The oil market remains in backwardation, a phenomenon that occurs where futures contracts with immediate or near-term deliveries sell at a premium over later deliveries, suggesting an expectation that prices will fall over time.
Equity markets have also largely shrugged off the potential ramifications of the conflict, with global stocks seeing a broad rally this year as corporate earnings optimism outweighed concerns about the war's implications for the world economy.
No breakthrough in sight
As the war neared the six-month milestone, Middle East experts told CNBC that while the nature of the conflict appeared to have shifted, a near-term breakthrough to bring the war to an end is unlikely.
"The conflict has lapsed into a standoff, with neither side apparently ready to escalate or make concessions," said Gregory Brew, a senior analyst specializing in Iran and energy at Eurasia Group.
Brew said the U.S. had backed away from escalating strikes on Iran, seemingly deterred by the risk of significant Iranian retaliation and concerns that another round of heavy fighting would further deplete munitions stockpiles.
"Instead, Trump has opted for a pressure campaign, a 'wait and see' approach, hoping that economic pressure compels the Iranians to capitulate," he told CNBC in an email — but he noted that a breakthrough "doesn't look imminent."
"It's unlikely to work," he said of Trump's so-called "Economic D-Day."
"Iran has been very resilient in the face of U.S. economic pressure, and while it faces the worst economic crisis since the 1980s," Brew added. "Its leadership is more likely to resist and escalate than to give in to U.S. demands."
Will Todman, a senior fellow with the CSIS Middle East Program, agreed that it appeared the U.S. had pivoted to a new strategy.
"The 'D-Day' announcement of secondary sanctions on Iran was the clearest sign that economic warfare is now the Trump administration's preferred strategy," he said. "However, there is little evidence to suggest that an economic-centric strategy will force the Iranians to capitulate or make more substantial concessions in talks."
Iran's economy squeezed
Steven A. Cook, Senior Fellow for Middle East and Africa Studies, Council on Foreign Relations, said the U.S. would likely respond militarily if any American ships or personnel are attacked, but added that the Iranian leadership is prepared to endure a lot of hardship and inflict a lot of pain on its own population.
"That suggests they will not give up or compromise so quickly," he said. "There is no telling how long this will go on. The president thought the war would last four to six weeks. He never expected them to resist effectively. The Iranians have now discovered the power of their geography and seem unwilling to give up on controlling/administering the Strait of Hormuz."
Dennis Ross, a former U.S. diplomat who served as the special Middle East coordinator under President Bill Clinton, told CNBC it seems clear for now that Trump does not want to resume all-out military operations.
"His new approach is to tighten the economic noose around the Iranians," he said.
However, Ross noted that over the years, the Iranian regime has "become good at workarounds and evasion of sanctions."
"But the combination of the blockade and what may be tighter enforcement of sanctions will put more pressure on an Iranian economy already in free fall," he said in an email. "That said, this Iranian leadership does not mind imposing hardship on its public and thinks it can outlast the president."
If the new approach is successful in squeezing the Iranian economy significantly more, he added, there was a good chance Tehran would escalate militarily or target its neighbors' ability to export.
Trump told Al Jazeera on Wednesday that he was prepared to continue the Iran war for as long as necessary. But experts said a lack of clarity on Washington's objectives made it difficult to quantify what would actually constitute mission accomplished for the White House.
Measuring success in the Iran war
"The Trump administration has still not defined what victory for the United States would look like, although it has articulated wide-reaching goals," CSIS's Todman said. "These range from ending Iran's nuclear program to opening the Strait of Hormuz to regime change. It is therefore impossible to determine if the U.S. can win or not."
He added that it was very unlikely Iran would make the concessions the president wants to see.
"They feel emboldened by their ability to withstand six months of war with the United States and Israel, despite having far inferior military capabilities."
Michael O'Hanlon, director of research in the Brookings Institution's Foreign Policy program, said Trump had "blundered in getting into a war with unrealistic expectations of what it would entail or how long it would last," and had settled on "the least bad option."
"Whether we win or lose in a zero-sum sense against Iran, we should worry about three central things and keep our eye on the ball: reducing, limiting [or] ending the violence, reopening Hormuz, and putting a long-term lid on Iran's nuclear program," O'Hanlon, who specializes in U.S. defense strategy, the use of military force, and American national security policy, added.
"If that happens, our core strategic objectives will be realized — whether we have bragging rights to have 'won' the war or not."

articles.title: Trump’s Greenland fixation puts security at the heart of Iceland’s knife-edge EU vote
articles.text:
Icelanders on Saturday will vote in a knife-edge referendum on whether to resume negotiations to join the European Union, reopening a debate that has taken on deeper significance in the wake of U.S. President Donald Trump's Arctic saber-rattling.
The question put to the Nordic nation of nearly 400,000 is simply: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"
Opinion polls indicate the advisory vote is likely to go down to the wire, with the country effectively split in half on the issue. If a majority of voters answer yes, accession negotiations will take place, which if successful, would lead to a negotiated agreement being put to a second referendum for the Icelandic people to accept or reject.
It comes as the Arctic emerges as a major hotbed for critical minerals and climate change rapidly melts sea ice, opening seasonal shipping routes, and amid Trump's renewed push to acquire Greenland, Iceland's closest neighbor.
The U.S. president has long advocated for control over Greenland on national security grounds. Notably, Trump appeared to repeatedly mix up Greenland and Iceland during a special address at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland earlier in the year.
"All of the arguments put forth by the U.S. president for why it would be necessary for the U.S. to acquire Greenland actually equally applied to Iceland. The only difference is that Iceland is formally an independent country," said Eiríkur Bergmann, professor of politics at Iceland's Bifröst University.
Read more
Iceland applied to join the EU in 2009 in the aftermath of the global financial crisis, before suspending membership talks in 2013 when a euroskeptic coalition government came to power.
At the start of the year, Iceland Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir said that deeper dialogue and collaboration with the EU would be a key factor in shoring up the country's interests.
"It is clear that the international system we have lived in since the end of World War II is in turmoil," Gunnarsdottir said in an article for Icelandic newspaper Visir, according to a Google translation.
Economy, sovereignty and fisheries
Alongside Trump's Greenland ambitions, Bergmann said diminishing trust in the U.S. as a security partner is another key concern ahead of the vote.
Iceland, a founding member of NATO, is the only ally that does not have its own military forces. The country also sits astride the so-called GIUK Gap, a naval choke point between Greenland, Iceland and the U.K. that links the Arctic to the Atlantic Ocean.
"Iceland's security and defense is guarded by our membership in NATO, but also, for many, more importantly, by a bilateral defense agreement with the U.S. since 1951. Now many people are sort of reconsidering the validity of that defense agreement," Bergmann said.
While these geopolitical developments have influenced the context in which Icelanders have discussed the prospect of EU membership, political experts have stressed the debate has primarily been driven by domestic issues — particularly the economy, sovereignty and fisheries.
One argument that is being made in favor of a yes vote concerns the Icelandic krona, a free-floating currency known to be vulnerable to sharp currency fluctuations.
"The current Social Democrat-led government, which actually initiated or applied for membership the first time round, is now reheating its bid to close this unfinished business, so to speak," Steven Blockmans, deputy director at the International Centre for Defence and Security think tank, told CNBC by telephone.
Former Icelandic Prime Minister Katrín Jakobsdóttir, meanwhile, has said that she doesn't see the argument for joining the EU, saying the country maintains close economic collaboration with the 27-nation bloc and its citizens already enjoy high living standards.
"If a majority of the people wants to apply, it is very important to listen to that majority, but I haven't changed my position," Jakobsdóttir told CNBC in mid-April.
To be sure, Iceland is already deeply integrated into the European framework, partly through its membership of the European Economic Area, which gives the volcanic island access to the EU's single market without requiring full membership.
Iceland is also a member of the Schengen Area, which allows passport-free travel between it and other participating European countries.
A success case for the EU?
For the EU, political experts have said the bloc is in the market for something of a success case, particularly after Britain's exit in 2020.
A victory for the yes campaign could pave the way for a negotiated agreement to be reached relatively quickly, Bergmann said, because Iceland's coalition government is approaching its next general election, which must be held no later than Aug. 2028.
"Bigger is better in this day and age, it seems," Blockmans said.
He added that the EU potentially welcoming a country ranked among the leading nations in GDP per capita and among the leading nations in global democratic performance would undoubtedly give "extra shine to the European integration project."

articles.title: CCTV Script 22/06/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JUNE 22, 2026.
For US equities, late June has typically been a slow period for earnings disclosures. Today, however, Wall Street has a new focus: Micron Technology. On Wednesday local time, Micron will report its third-quarter financial results for fiscal year 2026 after the market closes. Many market participants believe these results will serve as a crucial bellwether to test whether the AI rally can sustain its momentum.
Driven by artificial intelligence demand, memory chips are in short supply, pushing prices steadily higher and triggering explosive profit growth for Micron. At the same time, Micron has shifted a larger portion of its business toward high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, in recent years. Analysts note that HBM is becoming increasingly critical for AI applications while delivering significantly higher profit margins than traditional dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM.
Morningstar analysts point out that Micron's growth over the past year has been remarkable. Because this round of expansion was primarily driven by price increases, much of the additional revenue flowed straight to the bottom line.
Over the past 12 months, Micron's stock price has soared by more than 800%; year-to-date, it has already advanced nearly 300%.
MATT ORTON
Chief Market Strategist
Raymond James
"whether or not you think AI stocks are up too much, or there's still room to go. That's been the center of earnings momentum. So, Micron's results on Wednesday are going to be really important to help set the tone with respect to execution, where margins might be going for some of these bottleneck winners"
The market currently expects Micron to deliver strong results this week. However, the latest consensus estimates also suggest that the growth rate of Micron's adjusted earnings per share for the most recent quarter may be approaching its peak.
According to consensus estimates compiled by FactSet, the market expects Micron's adjusted EPS for the fiscal quarter ending in May to reach 20.57 dollars, representing a year-on-year increase of nearly 1,000%. Several analysts anticipate that Micron's performance could even top market expectations.
At the same time, market forecasts expect adjusted EPS growth for the following fiscal quarter ending in August to moderate to 725%.
Looking ahead one year, for the fiscal quarter also ending in May, market expectations show Micron's EPS could reach 31.7 dollars. While this absolute figure is noticeably higher than the 20.57 dollars expected for the current year, the year-on-year growth rate will decelerate to 54%.
Analysts also point out that Micron's performance is becoming increasingly significant for the S&P 500 index, the main benchmark for US equities.
Based on FactSet's definition of second-quarter reporting, which covers companies with fiscal quarters ending in May, June, or July, Nvidia and Micron are projected to be the largest contributors to the S&P 500's overall profit growth. Excluded Nvidia and Micron, the S&P 500's expected earnings growth rate would drop from roughly 22% down to 14.9%.
Finally, while the AI narrative dominates the market, underlying macroeconomic concerns persist. This week, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation metric, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, along with the final US first-quarter GDP reading, will also be released. Both reports will provide a vital pulse check on the health of the US consumer and the broader economy, and we will continue to keep you updated!

articles.title: CCTV Script 23/06/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JUNE 23, 2026.
Overnight, the British market's reaction to Keir Starmer's resignation remained relatively muted. Sterling and UK Gilts initially came under pressure before stabilizing, with analysts attributing the calm partly to the fact that the latest political turmoil had largely been priced in by the market. Looking at specific market metrics,
sterling dipped slightly against the US dollar, hovering around 1.324 dollars to the pound during early Asian trading this morning.
Since Starmer's political crisis began brewing in early May, the pound has fallen nearly 3% cumulative against the dollar.
In fixed income, the benchmark 10-year UK Gilt yield proved relatively stable, briefly edging up 1 basis point intraday to hit 4.85% before pulling back to hover around 4.81%.
In equities, the FTSE 100 index posted modest overnight gains, closing up 0.72%.
Why has the UK seen six prime ministers in ten years with such frequent leadership changes? Paul Johnson, former director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, attributes the root cause to sluggish economic growth.
A Financial Times analysis points out that the UK economy has never truly recovered since the 2008 financial crisis, with economic growth slowing more sharply post-2010 than in most other developed nations.
Johnson notes that successive prime ministers have taken a short-sighted approach to the UK's challenges, continually expanding public spending to soothe immediate pressures rather than pushing through politically difficult reforms to boost long-term growth.
As economic growth slowed, UK debt accumulated faster than in many other Western economies; before the financial crisis, UK public debt stood at roughly 30% of GDP, whereas today it hovers near 100%.
At present, markets have largely anticipated Andy Burnham succeeding Starmer. The real uncertainty centers on his future policy trajectory. Going forward, market focus will shift to Burnham's choice for Chancellor of the Exchequer, potential tweaks to fiscal rules, and the outlook for the upcoming Autumn Budget.
Kallum Pickering
Chief Economist
Peel Hunt
"Will the policies be inflationary? And, in my view, it's the inflationary side of British policy making over the past few years, which is really causing the problem in bond markets."
Analysts believe the key indicator to watch next is the direction of the UK Gilt market, noting that sentiment remains tense.
Ben Emons
Managing Director
Highline Asset Management
"If you're going the expansionary route, you know, and the burden could again face what Liz Truss phase two, you bring forward a package and it turns out to be the wrong package, it's wrongly timed and the bond market starts to gyrate, and then things fall apart, so it remains a very fluid situation, I think."

articles.title: Mixue shares extend slide after profit drop as ice cream-and-tea chain sees costs rise
articles.text:
Shares of Chinese ice cream and beverages chain Mixue Group fell more than 7% in Hong Kong on Friday, extending losses to a second straight session after the company reported a decline in first-half profit.
The stock closed 8.37% lower on Thursday, when Mixue reported that profit for the period fell 14.7% year on year to 2.32 billion yuan ($345.2 million) for the six months ended June. Revenue rose 2.3% to 15.22 billion yuan.
The company also proposed a special dividend of 2.65 yuan per share, subject to shareholder approval.
Mixue's profitability came under pressure from rising costs and expenses. Cost of sales grew faster than revenue, primarily due to investments aimed at improving product quality, while selling and distribution expenses jumped 22.9% on higher marketing and staff costs, the company said. Administrative expenses also rose 39.4%, mainly due to higher staff costs.
Mixue Group now has more stores globally than McDonald's and more than four times Dunkin's, with its store network totaling nearly 63,987 as of the end of June. The company is known for its affordable drinks and ice cream, including its signature King Cone vanilla ice cream.
While most of its stores are in mainland China, the company had 4,378 stores overseas as of end-June and has been expanding into new markets, including central Asia and the Americas.
Looking ahead, the company said it plans to deepen its presence in Southeast Asia and push further into central Asia and the Americas, while building a more localized supply chain to support its overseas expansion.
The company is also looking beyond drinks, with plans to turn its Snow King mascot into a global cultural brand through animated series, comics, movies, featured merchandise and even theme parks.

articles.title: OpenAI rolls out ads on select ChatGPT plans in India to boost monetization, support wider access
articles.text:
OpenAI has rolled out ads on ChatGPT for select plans in India, one of its largest and most active markets, as the artificial intelligence company looks to maximize its revenue ahead of its planned listing next year.
Advertising would support "broader access to ChatGPT through free and lower-cost tiers," a spokesperson for OpenAI told CNBC in an email. Ads have been rolled out for free users and those on the 399 rupee ($4) per month 'Go' plan.
The ad feature is already live in 38 countries, including the U.S., Japan, Korea and across 31 European nations, as per the information shared by the company.
"India is one of ChatGPT's largest and most active markets," the spokesperson said, adding that OpenAI's priority is to "learn from users and advertisers while protecting the experience that made ChatGPT valuable in the first place."
The company also added that it does not show ads to users who identify as, or are predicted by the algorithm to be under 18.
OpenAI is planning to go public in 2027 and faces pressure to justify its $852 billion valuation ahead of its IPO, especially as some of its key metrics lag behind its rival Anthropic, which is also preparing for listing on public markets.
Monetization through ads will help OpenAI partially cover the cost of generating inference for a query and stem the company's losses, experts said.
Unlike Anthropic, which gets a higher share of its revenues from enterprises, OpenAI is more popular among individual consumers, explained Ujjwal Chaudhry, a partner at market intelligence firm Analysys Mason.
To monetize an individual consumer base on a scale, the ad model is most effective, Chaudhry said, adding that his firm's data shows that online ads account for more than 75% of total global ad spending worth $1.18 trillion. In-app advertisements are a $400 billion market.
OpenAI told CNBC, "ads will be clearly labeled, visually separate and shown below the response," adding that "Answer independence is non-negotiable."
Earlier this year, Anthropic slammed OpenAI's plans to start showing ads, insisting that its chatbot Claude will remain ad-free. Users will not see ads or sponsored links near their conversations, and the chatbot's answers will not be influenced by third-party product placements, Anthropic had said.
"OpenAI is in a tough spot," Dan Niles, founder and portfolio manager at Niles Investment Management, told CNBC in June. OpenAI is going to get squeezed between Anthropic, which is focused on enterprise customers, and Google, which is "the king in consumer," Niles said, adding that Google has plenty of cash flow to fund its ambitions.
The ChatGPT-owner has rolled out managed ads feature in India, and on Sept. 4, it will launch self-serve ads. Self-serve ads are popular across many social media platforms as they allow advertisers to directly use the platform to bid for ad impressions, Chaudhry said.

articles.title: CCTV Script 24/06/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JUNE 24, 2026.
On Tuesday local time, the US semiconductor sector faced a sharp sell-off, with chip and memory stocks that had previously benefited heavily from the AI surge leading the declines and pulling the broader market down. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500 both closed at their lowest levels in nearly two weeks. Specifically, Micron and Sandisk both plummeted over 13% overnight, while AMD and Intel dropped by roughly 6%. Furthermore, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index retreated significantly from the record high set in the previous session, tumbling nearly 8% overnight to mark its largest single-day loss since June 5.
Analysts point out that this wave of global tech selling first erupted in the South Korean market. In the preceding session, the KOSPI index crashed nearly 10%, driven by a combination of fears over leveraged product risks and profit-taking by investors at market highs. The selling pressure subsequently spilled over into global markets. As for the pullback in US equities, some analysts attribute it partly to AI trades becoming overly crowded.
Andrew Slimmon
Managing Director
Morgan Stanley Investment Management
"They're crowded, in other words, it's captured the kind of zeitgeist of the momentum traders, and when that happens, you're going to have sharp sell-offs, like we're having."
In addition, leveraged products have amplified market volatility to some extent. In US equities, following the sharp pullback in semiconductor stocks, traders rapidly flocked to 3x inverse semiconductor ETFs, betting that the sector could fall further. Data from Charles Schwab's ThinkOrSwim platform shows that during overnight trading, option volume for Direxion's Daily Semiconductor Bear 3X Shares reached more than triple its daily average over the past month.
Finally, market concerns are extending from trading mechanics to core fundamentals. An increasing number of investors are paying attention to how tech giants are relying more heavily on debt financing to fund their AI expansion. Analysts warn that beyond crowded positioning and technical pullbacks, fundamental risks within the AI supply chain may also be emerging.
Analysts note that as capital expenditure for AI and cloud infrastructure expands, corporate funding mechanisms are shifting. SpaceX initiated a bond offering this week as the latest example, following Alphabet, which has raised capital through global debt markets multiple times.
At the same time, markets have recently ramped up bets on a Fed rate hike later this year. Analysts warn that if tech companies rely increasingly on debt to fund AI expansion, higher interest rates could drive up borrowing costs. This means investor scrutiny will extend beyond the sheer scale of AI investment to encompass debt burdens, capital costs, and return timelines.
Dan Skelly
Managing Director
Morgan Stanley Wealth Management
"We've heard about pricing wars among some of the model builders, we've heard about rental prices for old GPUs starting to decline, and we've also seen a shift in tone from Microsoft, who led the AI kind of launch three years ago with Chat GPT and their partnership with Open AI, Microsoft now talking about a change in strategic direction for lower-cost models."

articles.title: CCTV Script 25/06/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JUNE 25, 2026.
Oil shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz have rebounded significantly. According to data from commodities analytics firm Kpler, since the United States and Iran reached an agreement, at least 20 tankers carrying 35 million barrels of crude oil—previously stranded in the Persian Gulf—have successfully transited out through the Strait of Hormuz.
Kpler's data further indicates that oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to approximately 4.8 million barrels per day since the US-Iran deal was struck. June oil flows also rose to their highest level since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28. However, it is worth noting that export volumes remain far below pre-conflict levels, which previously saw around 15 million barrels of oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz daily.
As crude exports rebound, security risks in the Strait of Hormuz have eased accordingly.
The Joint Maritime Information Center, a US-led multinational naval advisory group, has downgraded the threat level for vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz from the highest status of "Critical" to "Moderate." In its latest advisory published this week, the center stated that while attacks remain possible, they are unlikely, as overall risk has receded following the implementation of the US-Iran memorandum of understanding.
As markets digest the easing of shipping disruption fears in the Strait of Hormuz, international oil prices have posted noticeable declines. At the same time, however, Trump has directed criticism at US oil companies, faulting them for not lowering retail gasoline prices quickly enough.
According to data from the AAA, the national average retail gas price in the US stood at approximately $3.93 per gallon as of Wednesday, remaining elevated above five-year historical averages for this period.
As illustrated in this chart, following the outbreak of the Middle East conflict in late February, both WTI crude oil prices and US retail gas prices surged in tandem. However, entering June, crude prices pulled back significantly, while retail gasoline prices declined at a markedly slower pace.
Addressing this disparity, Trump posted on Wednesday local time stating that while purchasing costs for crude oil paid by major oil companies have fallen sharply, they have failed to pass those savings on at the pump. Trump added that he has directed the Department of Justice to investigate the matter.
However, experts told CNBC that a natural time lag exists when price changes transmit from crude oil to retail gasoline.
Karen Young
Senior Research Scholar
Center on Global Energy Policy, Columbia University
"There are state and local taxes, which are applied to the price of gas at stations in the United States, and it really is up to refiners, and it takes a couple of weeks before crude prices drop, that then the prices at refineries, and then on to eventually consumers can really respond."
Finally, looking ahead at crude price trends, energy expert Daniel Yergin noted that although the strait crisis has eased, considerable uncertainty remains surrounding long-term transit arrangements and toll disputes.
Daniel Yergin
Vice Chairman
S&P Global
"We're not back to where we were at the beginning of the year, when it was expected there was going to be a huge glut of oil, and prices, you know, we're in the low 60s, so with all the insecurity, it seems 70 to 85 seems a reasonable range, unless something dramatically changes."

articles.title: CCTV Script 26/06/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JUNE 26, 2026.
On Thursday local time, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee stated in an interview with CNBC that while the latest PCE inflation report delivered positive signals, overall price pressures remain elevated. In particular, the core inflation trend has yet to improve, which he views as the single greatest challenge currently.
Austan Goolsbee
President
Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
"Right now, as between the two sides of the Fed's mandate, the inflation side and the job market side, clearly the problems on the inflation side."
Additionally, Goolsbee expressed support for new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's efforts to reform Federal Reserve communication. He noted that Warsh brings fresh perspectives and that he personally favors streamlining communications, curbing forward guidance, and refraining from speculating on future interest rate paths.
Markets are currently coalescing around a prevailing scenario: the Federal Reserve will likely hold rates steady in July and is more probable to enact a rate hike in September.
According to the CME FedWatch Tool, market pricing assigns a nearly 70% probability to the Fed keeping interest rates unchanged at its July meeting.
Looking out to September, the market places a 36.6% probability on the Fed keeping rates at current levels, with a higher likelihood pointing toward interest rates moving upward.
In terms of market reaction, because the latest inflation report aligned closely with prior expectations, it failed to trigger widespread panic, leaving US equity moves relatively subdued overnight.
All three major US stock indexes moved by less than 0.5% overnight: the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.14%, the S&P 500 dipped about 0.01%, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.46%.
Investor attention is currently shifting toward a growing divergence within technology equities, as market capital rotates away from mega-cap tech giants and into the AI infrastructure supply chain.
Overnight, both Apple and Microsoft traded lower after raising product prices in response to escalating memory costs. Conversely, the beneficiaries of those higher prices—namely the memory chip sector—experienced a renewed surge of buying interest.
Analysts observe that market anxiety surrounding mega-cap tech companies has escalated markedly in recent weeks. Although hyperscalers such as Microsoft and Alphabet continue to drive the bulk of AI deployment, investors worry that capital expenditures have expanded dramatically while full commercial monetization remains 6 to 9 months away. Consequently, investors are shifting focus from the entities funding the infrastructure to those collecting the revenue, favoring AI infrastructure providers that can realize order books and revenue streams sooner.
Dan Ives
Global Head of Technology Research
Wedbush Securities
"It's almost like they're funding the AI party, but the ones that are benefiting are from memory to chip to supply chain to some of the infrastructure players."
Stephanie Link
Chief Investment Strategist
Hightower Advisors
"The industrial companies are definitely the winners, for sure. We know data centers take three years to build, 40 billion for one gigawatt plant. So, there's a lot that goes inside of data centers, and those are the winners, too."

articles.title: CCTV Weekly Script 26/06/26
articles.text:
– This is the weekly script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JUNE 26, 2026.
Our first feature profile this week focuses on Cristiano Ronaldo, often referred to simply as CR7.
This week, the 41-year-old Ronaldo made history. In Portugal's 5-0 victory over Uzbekistan, Ronaldo scored a brace, becoming the first player in history to score in six consecutive World Cups. After the final whistle, he shouted "I'm back" at the camera, seemingly responding to doubts from critics following Portugal's draw in their opening match. Portugal manager Roberto Martínez emphasized that what makes Ronaldo truly impressive is how he responds under pressure: even when emotions run high, he returns to the training pitch, puts in the work, and continues pushing forward. It is precisely this professionalism that has fueled his longevity.
At the same time, Ronaldo remains one of the most commercially valuable athletes in global sports. He boasts over 600 million followers on Instagram alongside a massive roster of sponsors. According to Forbes' 2026 list of the world's highest-paid athletes, Ronaldo earned approximately $300 million over the past 12 months, topping the list for the fourth consecutive year and the sixth time overall. Analysts point out that this is very likely the final World Cup of Ronaldo's career. Attention is now focused on whether he can lead Portugal in a run for the World Cup title, as well as how this elite athlete will position himself off the pitch moving forward.
Turning next to the UK, 56-year-old Andy Burnham, a frontrunner to become the next British Prime Minister, became a key focus for markets this week. Should he assume the prime ministership as expected, the biggest financial story will be a potential shift in the UK's economic governance route. Dubbed the "King of the North" by British media, Burnham has long advocated for "Britain beyond London." His core economic platform focuses on reshaping Britain's growth model through regional devolution, skills system reforms, and regional re-industrialization.
Burnham's latest and most striking vision is moving part of 10 Downing Street's functions to Manchester to create a "Northern 10 Downing Street." This is viewed as part of his decentralization agenda, aiming to transfer powers in areas such as skills training and select tax authorities from London to local combined authorities. Additionally, analysts note that one of Burnham's immediate major challenges will be fiscal hurdles. The UK tax burden has reached historic highs, and if the new government intends to generate further fiscal revenue, it will find it difficult to avoid impacting middle-income earners.
Finally, markets this week paid close attention to news of the passing of former Federal Reserve Chair Alan Greenspan. Greenspan was one of the most iconic central banking figures in post-WWII American history. He steered the Federal Reserve through the 1987 stock market crash, the Asian financial crisis, and the bursting of the dot-com bubble, though his legacy faced renewed scrutiny following the 2008 financial crisis. Notably, newly appointed Fed Chair Kevin Warsh cited Greenspan multiple times during his swearing-in ceremony, referring to him as a role model. Re-examining Greenspan's policy legacy may help us better understand the policy trade-offs facing today's Federal Reserve.
Greenspan was renowned for his formidable data-crunching capabilities, sharp reading of market psychology, and subtle, often elusive communication style. The resemblance between Warsh and Greenspan lies not in simplistic "hawkish" or "dovish" labels, but in their policy approach: both place heavy emphasis on market signals, prioritize central bank credibility, and believe technological advancements can alter the relationship between economic growth and inflation. Analysts suggest that for today's Fed, Greenspan's legacy serves as both inspiration and caution: the AI era may require reassessing the relationship between productivity and inflation, but ignoring financial risks and leverage accumulation leaves the Fed vulnerable to underestimating the costs of a bursting bubble.
That concludes this week's key newsmakers. We will continue to follow these stories for you.

articles.title: CCTV Script 02/07/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JULY 02, 2026.
Starting first with Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, he once again emphasized his opposition to forward guidance, calling on central banks to return to first principles when making policy decisions. In fact, throughout the entire panel discussion, "forward guidance" itself became a recurring joke among several central bank governors. Whenever the moderator attempted to prompt the governors to signal their next policy moves, they all avoided, downplayed, or outright rejected doing so in various ways.
Analysis from Bank of America shows that Fed officials already appear to be adapting to Warsh's latest communication style by cutting back on public appearances. According to Bank of America's tracking, since the June Fed policy meeting, including events scheduled through this week, Fed officials have made a total of only 12 speeches and interviews. By comparison, prior to Warsh taking office, officials averaged roughly 23 public appearances during the same two-week period following each Fed policy meeting since 2022.
Additionally, some analysts are attempting to project the Fed's policy trajectory based on Warsh's outlook on AI.
Randall Kroszner
Former Fed Governor
"Kevin thinks this is going to be productivity enhancing and also ultimately wage enhancing and that, but wage enhancing because of higher productivity growth, and that's actually allow give him a basis for potentially cutting rates rather than raising rates."
Meanwhile, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde stated that the ECB decided early on to abandon forward guidance. She emphasized that what truly matters is helping the market understand how the central bank forms its monetary policy stance, describing this approach as "framework guidance" rather than letting the market blindly rely on specific forecasts.
The market's current focus is on the latest inflation report from the eurozone. Data shows that eurozone inflation fell from 3.2% in May to 2.8% in June, coming in below the market expectation of 3%. This reduces the urgency for the ECB to continue raising interest rates in July, with markets now leaning toward the view that the ECB will hold rates steady this month. However, market participants still believe the ECB could act again in September or October.
Finally, regarding Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey, his tone has skewed dovish in recent months, favoring a wait-and-see approach to the impact of the Middle East conflict.
Furthermore, Bailey stated that simply not cutting rates already constitutes monetary policy tightening.
Andrew Bailey
Governor of the Bank of England
"The markets were expecting a couple of cuts this year. And I'd said a number of times I didn't think that was unreasonable. So, back in March, we really had to take that off the table, which we did. So, you can sort of think of that as a tightening."
Markets have now drastically scaled back bets on Bank of England rate hikes, with current market pricing suggesting less than 25 basis points of total tightening from the BOE this year. However, some analysts remain concerned about second-order effects from the Middle East conflict, and we will continue to keep a close watch on developments for you.

articles.title: CCTV Script 03/07/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JULY 03, 2026.
According to data released by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics on Thursday local time, the US unemployment rate in June fell to 4.2%, its lowest level in a year. While this figure appears to add a bright spot to an otherwise weak employment report, the underlying cause is far from encouraging.
Analysts point out that the drop in the unemployment rate stems from a large number of American workers leaving the labor force, rather than any strengthening in the job market. Data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that the US labor force participation rate fell to 61.5% in June, marking its lowest point since March 2021. This metric measures the proportion of the working-age population that is either employed or actively seeking employment.
Declines in the US labor force participation rate are sometimes attributed to reduced immigration, as well as the ongoing retirement of Baby Boomers and Generation X—specifically individuals currently aged 62 to 80 and 46 to 61. However, the largest drop in June occurred among prime-age workers, leaving several economists puzzled and surprised.
Jan Hatzius
Chief Economist
Goldman Sachs
"In this number, the participation rate plunge among 25 to 34 year olds. I mean, there's not a lot of precedent for these kinds of moves month to month. The household surveys always noisy, but this is very, very large."
The chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management told CNBC that the latest data indicates the US labor market is not overheating. This may offer Fed Chair Kevin Warsh a moment of relief, as it implies the Federal Reserve has room to hold rates steady throughout the summer if it chooses. Consequently, markets have already trimmed their Fed rate hike expectations.
Data from the CME FedWatch Tool shows that while there was roughly a 64% probability priced in yesterday for a Fed rate hike in September, those rate hike bets cooled rapidly. Meanwhile, the probability of the Fed standing pat rose from nearly 36% to almost 47%.
Beyond employment, turning to the other side of the Fed's dual mandate—inflation. As Americans prepare for an upcoming three-day long weekend, economists warn that hosting a July 4th holiday cookout this year could cost nearly 10% more than last year.
Taking hot dogs, a common American staple, as an example: data from retail data provider Datasembly shows that an 8-pack of hot dog buns is up over 12% year-over-year, an 8-pack of beef hot dog sausages has jumped nearly 18% year-over-year, and ketchup to top the hot dogs is up roughly 7% year-over-year.
Estimates from the American Farm Bureau Federation show that hosting a party for 10 people this year will cost an American household approximately $73.82, or around 501 RMB. According to Datasembly's figures, this year's cookout bill will be 9.4% higher than last year's.

articles.title: Iran links Hormuz reopening to ending regional wars as Trump reportedly rejects return to June deal
articles.text:
Iran has set out its conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, saying that ending the wars in the Middle East was among them.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told Lebanese media outlet Al Manar TV that any understanding on the strait with the U.S. will include an end to wars and military operations in Lebanon, Gaza and Syria.
He added the conflict in the Gaza Strip has to end, while demanding that Israel withdraw from Lebanon and halt attacks on Syria.
Rezaei said that the Strait of Hormuz cannot be separated from the broader regional conflict, adding that the U.S. must "prove its seriousness" in implementing the these commitments "before any new trust could be established."
However, a return to diplomacy does not seem imminent. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the Trump administration has no interest in going back to the terms of the memorandum of understanding it reached with Iran in June.
Citing people familiar with the matter, the Journal said that U.S. President Donald Trump was no longer interested in the June deal framework, and is instead waiting to see if his administration's strategy of pressuring Iran economically will work.
The U.S. on Monday announced an "economic D-Day" campaign against Teheran, threatening countries that do business with the Islamic Republic, shifting its focus from military action to economic pressure.
Temporary relief
Iran is now allowing a "temporary and limited" corridor for ships to pass through the Hormuz Strait, and the future of maritime traffic will depend on developments in understandings with Washington, according to Rezaei.
Earlier this week, Oman and Iran discussed a proposal to establish a temporary joint shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz as well as a mission to clear mines from the key oil export corridor.
However, a video posted on X late Thursday stateside by Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command credited U.S. forces for clearing the mines from the strait.
Centcom forces have helped facilitate the transit of approximately 1,500 commercial vessels and 750 million barrels of crude oil over the past several months, Cooper said. "Today, international shipping lanes are open, and momentum is building."
However, the latest available Kpler data showed that only five ships crossed Hormuz on Tuesday, a far cry from the approximately 130 ships that used to transit the crucial waterway before the war broke out in February.

articles.title: Judge blocks Pentagon blacklist of Anthropic as supply chain risk
articles.text:
A San Francisco federal judge on Thursday ruled that the Pentagon's blacklisting of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic earlier this year was illegal.
U.S. District Judge Rita Lin found that the Department of Defense violated the First Amendment by designating Anthropic a supply chain risk "based on a desire to make a public example" out of the company. Lin wrote that while the government is owed deference on matters of national security, its actions were not founded on any "articulable basis."
"Defendants claim that because of Anthropic's 'increasingly hostile manner through the press' and its criticism of the Department of War's views on AI use, Defendants 'cannot trust Anthropic to ensure the integrity of its models,' " Lin wrote in her order. "Neither the Constitution nor the federal statute invoked by Defendants allows them to impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic's critique of the Administration's views."
In March, the DOD designated Anthropic a supply chain risk, meaning the company purportedly threatened U.S. national security, after negotiations about how the military could use its Claude AI models spiraled out of control.
Anthropic wanted assurance that its technology would not be used for fully autonomous weapons or domestic mass surveillance, and the DOD wanted Anthropic to grant the agency unfettered access to Claude across all lawful purposes.
Talks escalated and then collapsed, and Anthropic became the first American company to publicly be named a supply chain risk. The designation barred defense contractors from using Anthropic's technology in their work with the agency.
Anthropic sued the Trump administration in San Francisco and Washington, D.C., an effort to reverse its blacklisting. The DOD relied on two distinct designations to justify its supply chain risk action, which meant they had to be litigated in two separate courts.
Lin's ruling on Thursday handed Anthropic a major victory, but the company's litigation in D.C. is still ongoing. Until that case is resolved, Anthropic still technically remains a supply chain risk.
In a statement, Anthropic praised Lin's decision.
"We welcome the court's ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful," a spokesperson told CNBC. "We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology."
The ruling clears a significant hurdle for Anthropic as it marches toward what's expected to be a near-record IPO. While the company has shown no signs of a slowdown since the blacklisting, if it's able to reestablish ties with the Pentagon, it could open additional business opportunities that had been cut off.
Anthropic has said it brought the lawsuits an effort to return its business to the status quo before it was designated a supply chain risk. The suits would not require the Pentagon to restart its work with the company.
WATCH: Department of Defense Under Secretary: Evident by Anthropic’s actions it was a ‘supply chain risk’

articles.title: CCTV Weekly Script 03/07/26
articles.text:
– This is the weekly script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JULY 03, 2026.
Our first feature profile this week focuses on Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra.
Against the backdrop of broader pressure on technology stocks this week, Micron's stock price also pulled back significantly. However, it is worth noting that the prices of memory chips sold by Micron continue to rise. In an exclusive interview with CNBC this week, Mehrotra explained a major reason behind the current memory chip supply shortage from an industry insider perspective: before the full explosion of AI demand, the memory industry faced prolonged price pressure from customers, particularly around 2023.
SANJAY MEHROTRA
CEO
MICRON
"Certain customers drove pricing significantly down in our industry, and that, of course, resulted in significant negative gross margins for certain customers, certain products, and that really impacted the investment capability of the industry."
Underinvestment in the industry over past years has resulted in supply capability failing to keep pace today. Mehrotra stated that Micron's current advantageous position stems from the company's commitment to continuous investment even during industry downturns. However, he indicated that the tight supply of memory chips could persist beyond 2027, as constructing new semiconductor fabs takes several years and the manufacturing complexity of next-generation memory chips is increasing significantly.
Turning to Europe, several economists warned about the risk factors surrounding the AI surge at the European Central Bank's Forum on Central Banking in Portugal this week. Among the prominent figures was Tobias Adrian, Director of the Monetary and Capital Markets Department at the International Monetary Fund. He emphasized that his primary concern lies in the leverage being added by both borrowers and investors when betting on the AI boom, which could create hidden risks for financial stability.
Tobias Adrian
Director, Monetary and Capital Markets Department
IMF
"On the risk side, is this risk that profits may disappoint. There's a lot of concentration risk in the technology sector, a lot of risk in a small number of firms. You know, could that lead to broader fallout?"
Adrian noted that while earnings for AI-related enterprises remain strong, a growing number of data centers and cloud computing platforms are relying on debt financing. The issue is that AI technology iterates extremely fast, causing related equipment and computing assets to depreciate rapidly, whereas financing debts are long term, creating a maturity mismatch risk.
Some market participants are already taking action by betting on a cooling AI frenzy. Finally, we turn to key newsmaker Michael Burry, the renowned investor and real-life inspiration for "The Big Short." This week, Burry further expanded his short positions against the AI supply chain. He revealed that he has shorted industrial equipment manufacturer Caterpillar, while building new bearish positions against Nvidia, semiconductor equipment manufacturer Applied Materials, Tesla, and an ETF tracking the US semiconductor index.
Burry has been a vocal critic of AI mania in the stock market, arguing that the rally in AI-related equities is becoming overextended. He pointed out that the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index currently trades about 65% above its 200-day moving average, a level he noted was previously seen only during the 2000 dot-com bubble. Furthermore, he believes that South Korea's announcement this week of massive spending plans for the AI industry ignited short-term market enthusiasm, but in Burry's view, this precisely signals that the AI boom is beginning to near its end.
That concludes this week's key newsmakers. We will continue to follow these stories for you.

articles.title: Trump ratchets up rhetoric against Beijing as U.S.-China officials meet for Xi's Washington visit
articles.text:
BEIJING — As the U.S. ramped up pressure this week on China with secondary Iran sanctions, the world's two largest economies have still managed to stay focused on ways to cooperate.
It's a sign of the balancing act on both sides, even as White House rhetoric has remained tough.
U.S. President Donald Trump signaled to reporters Thursday local time he could be sanctioning Chinese banks. "I don't have to announce everything," he said, according to a Fox News stream of the event.
Those comments followed a meeting between U.S. and Chinese officials in Beijing on Wednesday, according to official announcements.
U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue said in a social media post that he met with China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi and three other Chinese officials to discuss President Xi Jinping's upcoming state visit to Washington.
China's readout also noted Perdue's comment on "preparing well for the next stage of important high-level interactions," according to a CNBC translation of Chinese.
Trump on Thursday even mentioned Xi was coming in a few weeks.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday had warned that if Chinese banks "are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted." It was part of Trump's "economic D-Day" announcements against Iran.
Other than Bessent's comments, there few details on specific actions, said Jodie Wen, postdoctoral fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy (CISS), Tsinghua University. It's more of a warning, she said.
Wen added that the Trump-Xi summit in May marked a shift toward controlled competition, rather than the Biden administration's "strategic adversary" view on China.
Moderate response
China's official response to U.S. secondary Iran sanctions has also been muted so far.
Beijing responded by saying it would "take all necessary measures" to protect itself, but did not elaborate on possible actions. When asked about communication with the U.S. on Iran, a foreign ministry spokesperson said there was no information to share.
However, the spokesperson said the two countries were in talks about a Trump-Xi meeting.
Beijing will "note the lack of groundwork that was laid ahead of Bessent's 'D-Day' announcement. And they will conclude that this is largely performative," Ryan Hass, director of the China center and Chair in Taiwan studies at Brookings, said in a social media post. Hass advised the Obama administration as director for China, Taiwan and Mongolia for the National Security Council.
"Sec. Bessent already basically gave away the game when he responded to a question by asking, 'Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?' Beijing will interpret this as signaling that the US is not going to go after major Chinese financial institutions," Hass said.
He expects the U.S.-China trade truce to remain intact because the "alternative is worse for both sides."
Beijing can also comply with U.S. sanctions and its own interests at the same time.
The Asian country has built a legal mechanism that essentially tells Chinese companies their foreign bankers must comply with U.S. rules, but inside China, Beijing's law takes precedence, said Han Shen Lin, China managing director for The Asia Group and a former executive at Wells Fargo Bank in China.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

articles.title: CCTV Script 06/07/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on JULY 06, 2026.
First in the US, over the past three-day long weekend, an extreme heatwave driven by the "heat dome" effect swept across several densely populated regions in the central and eastern parts of the country. The extreme heat pushed up air conditioning electricity demand, while heavy storms simultaneously dealt a blow to power supplies in parts of the country.
According to data from power outage tracking site PowerOutage.com, as of Sunday morning local time, nearly 1 million homes were without power across more than ten US states. By Sunday evening local time, around 720,000 homes remained without power, with the most severe outages concentrated in parts of the US Northeast and Midwest. Specifically, about 127,000 homes in Michigan, 123,000 in Pennsylvania, and 62,000 in New Jersey were still affected.
This chart shows the 24-hour moving average load for PJM Interconnection, a major regional transmission organization in the US, which can be understood as the average electricity demand placed on the grid over the past day. As shown on the chart, the load curve in 2026 surged significantly in late June, briefly exceeding 125,000 megawatts.
Analysts note that driven by the heatwave, PJM's recent grid load has been visibly higher than the levels recorded during the same period over the past two summers. Extreme heat is set to further exacerbate upward pressure on electricity prices in parts of the US.
Turning to Asia, HSBC's Chief Asia Economist told CNBC in an interview that this year's El Niño phenomenon could impact Asian agricultural output and further push up food prices, serving as a major inflation risk for Asia in the second half of the year.
